sections.b: At the last supper Jesus gets up from the meal, strips to a towel and washes his disciples' feet, the work of a slave (John 13:1–17). Peter refuses until Jesus says, "Unless I wash you, you will have no place with me." Jesus then explains the act as a model: since their Lord and Teacher has washed their feet, they owe it to one another to do the same. The verbs for setting aside and taking up his clothes are those he used for laying down and taking up his life (John 10:17–18), so the scene also points to his death.

common: Jesus washed feet to teach humility and service.
uncommon: John Christopher Thomas argues that John's community washed feet as a rite of forgiveness for sins committed after baptism.

sections.b: After Judas leaves (John 13:30), Jesus speaks to the eleven at length: he is going to the Father; they must love one another; he will send another Advocate; he is the vine and they are branches; the world will hate them; their grief will turn to joy. He ends with a prayer for himself, for them and for all who will believe (John 17). The words "Get up. Let us leave this place" (John 14:31) in the middle suggest to many scholars that the speech grew in stages, with 16:4b–33 as a second version of chapter 14.

claude.title: Claude's theory: the speech mirrors Deuteronomy
claude.body: Deuteronomy is Moses's farewell on the edge of a land he will not enter, given to a people who will go on without him, with a promise of a prophet like him (Deuteronomy 18:15) and a closing song and blessing. John 13–17 has the same shape: the departing leader, love and commands as the condition of remaining, a successor (the Advocate) who speaks what he hears (Deuteronomy 18:18; John 16:13), and a closing prayer. If John modeled the discourse on Deuteronomy, the Advocate plays Joshua's role and the disciples are Israel on the plains of Moab. Scholars have noted Deuteronomy echoes in John (for example A. Lacomara), so this is an extension of published work, not a new claim.

sections.h: Judas at the last supper in John
sections.b: John says the devil had already planted the plan (John 13:2). Jesus washes Judas's feet with the rest, quotes Psalm 41:9 about the friend who eats his bread and turns on him, and gives Judas a dipped piece of bread, a gesture of honor. Then "Satan went into him," and Judas goes out into the night (John 13:27–30). In his prayer Jesus calls him "the son of ruin" (John 17:12).

sections.h: The farewell discourse and the Trinity
sections.b: John 14–17 says the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father (John 14:10–11), that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father (John 14:9), that the Father sends the Spirit in the Son's name (John 14:26) while the Son sends him from the Father (John 15:26), and that the Spirit takes from what is the Son's because all that the Father has is the Son's (John 16:14–15). The Father is also "greater" (John 14:28). The Nicene fathers, Arius, and later the debate over the Filioque all argued from these verses.

Jesus promises "another Advocate" (paraklētos), the Spirit of truth, who will remain with the disciples and be in them (John 14:16–17), teach them and remind them of his words (John 14:26), bear witness about him (John 15:26), expose the world's error about sin, righteousness and judgment (John 16:8–11) and lead them in all the truth (John 16:13). The Spirit comes only after Jesus goes (John 16:7). John 15:26, "who proceeds from the Father," is the source of the creed's "proceeds from the Father" and of the Filioque dispute.

common: The Advocate is the Holy Spirit, a Person, sent to continue Jesus's presence.
uncommon: Some Muslim writers read the promised Advocate as a prophecy of Muhammad.

sections.h: A new command: as I loved you
sections.b: Jesus gives a "new command": love one another as he loved them (John 13:34–35; 15:12, 17). The standard is now his own love, which lays down its life for friends (John 15:13), and this love is the mark by which all will recognize his disciples. 1 John calls it both an old and a new command (1 John 2:7–8).

"I am the real vine, and my Father is the farmer" (John 15:1). Jesus takes Israel's image (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7) for himself. Branches that bear no fruit are taken away; fruitful ones are pruned clean; the command is to remain in him, because without him they can do nothing (John 15:1–8).

sections.h: The branch that is thrown out
sections.b: "Whoever does not remain in me is tossed out like the branch and dries up" (John 15:6). Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Wesleyan readers take it as a real warning to real believers. Reformed and many Baptist readers see a branch that was attached only outwardly, like Judas, and point to promises that no one will snatch Jesus's sheep from his hand (John 10:28–29).

sections.h: Asking in Jesus's name; the prayer of John 17
sections.b: Jesus promises that whatever the disciples ask in his name will be done (John 14:13–14; 15:7, 16; 16:23–24), because the Father himself loves them (John 16:27). Then he prays aloud for himself, for his disciples and for all future believers (John 17), a prayer often called the High Priestly Prayer.

In John 17 Jesus intercedes for the disciples: keep them in your name, keep them from the evil one, make them holy in the truth, and make them one. He also prays for all who will believe through their word (John 17:20). Yet he says the disciples will not need him to ask the Father for them, because the Father himself loves them (John 16:26–27).

When Judas goes out, Jesus says, "Now the Son of Man has been glorified" (John 13:31). In John, the cross is the moment of glory. In his prayer Jesus asks the Father to glorify him with the glory he had before the world existed (John 17:5), and he gives that glory to his disciples so that they may be one (John 17:22, 24).

sections.h: "The Father is greater than I am"
sections.b: John 14:28 was a key text for Arius, who said the Son was created. Gregory of Nazianzus answered that the Father is greater as source, Augustine that the Son speaks as man. The same chapter says that whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father (John 14:9), and John 17:5 speaks of the Son's glory with the Father before the world.

The devil plants the plan to hand Jesus over, and Satan enters Judas (John 13:2, 27). Jesus calls him "this world's ruler," who owns nothing in him (John 14:30) and has already been judged (John 16:11). Jesus prays that the disciples be kept from the evil one (John 17:15).

sections.h: "He will lead you in all the truth"
sections.b: Jesus promises that the Spirit will remind the disciples of his words (John 14:26) and lead them in all the truth (John 16:13). Catholics and Orthodox read the promise as continuing in the church's teaching and councils; Protestants as fulfilled in the apostles' witness preserved in Scripture, by which all later teaching is tested.

Jesus prays that believers will be in the Father and the Son (John 17:21) and says the Father and he will make their dwelling with whoever loves him (John 14:23). He gives them the glory the Father gave him (John 17:22). Orthodox theology reads these verses as theosis.

In John 14:3 Jesus promises to come again and take the disciples to himself. Readers take it as the Second Coming, the rapture (dispensationalists), the believer's death, or his coming at Easter and in the Spirit (John 14:18, 23). The "short time" sayings of John 16:16–22 are read in similar ways.

"It was not you who chose me. I chose you" (John 15:16; compare 13:18; 15:19). Wesleyan readers take it as choice for apostleship and mission, since Judas too was chosen (John 6:70); Reformed readers also see God's initiative in salvation.

Jesus warns that the world will hate and persecute the disciples as it did him, that they will be thrown out of the synagogue, and that people will kill them thinking they serve God (John 15:18–16:4). The Spirit and the disciples will be witnesses together (John 15:26–27).

"The Jews" appears only once in the farewell discourse (John 13:33), for Jesus's opponents in Jerusalem. But the speech speaks of "their law" (John 15:25) and of expulsion from the synagogue and death (John 16:2), lines that have been read as anti-Jewish. J. Louis Martyn tied 16:2 to the Birkat ha-Minim; Reuven Kimelman, Daniel Boyarin and Adele Reinhartz question or complicate that link.

The Beloved Disciple first appears at the last supper, reclining in Jesus's embrace (John 13:23), as Jesus is in the Father's (John 1:18). He returns at the cross, the tomb and the lake, and the Gospel names him as its witness (John 19:35; 21:24).

John sets the last supper "before the Passover festival" (John 13:1) and the crucifixion on the day of preparation (John 19:14), when the lambs were killed, unlike the Synoptic Gospels, where the supper is the Passover meal.

sections.h: "I have won the victory over the world"
sections.b: The night before his death, Jesus speaks of his victory as already won (John 16:33), the root of the promises to "the one who wins the victory" in Revelation and of 1 John 5:4–5.
